All reads are inside the repository; none is out of bounds. A read outside the repository would have changed this.

question: ADR-002 item 3 and PRD v2 Demo accounts leave timeZone's machine-checked shape open: what does the schema accept for the profile's timeZone?

options.label: booking-api@v1's room timeZone pattern
options.consequence: A string matching ^[A-Za-z_]+(/[A-Za-z0-9_+-]+)+$, the pattern booking-api@v1 already uses for a room's timeZone: an offset, an abbreviation, a bare city or an empty string fails the producer's replay; any IANA Area/Location name passes, so a third office needs no schema change. A name without a slash (UTC) fails, which no built-in account uses.

options.label: any non-empty string
options.consequence: The loosest check: Jakarta, WIB or +07:00 pass the replay, and the profile's zone and a room's zone could be the same kind of value in name only.

options.label: an enum of Asia/Jakarta and Europe/London
options.consequence: The tightest check, but a third office's zone becomes a schema change, and a consumer that switches exhaustively on the enum can break on it, which additive-only forbids.

chosen: booking-api@v1's room timeZone pattern
why: ADR-002 item 7 compares a room's timeZone with the user's as names, so both contracts should accept the same kind of value; reusing the pattern booking-api@v1's schema already carries keeps them one shape without a shared code package. The enum would turn a new office into a schema change a consumer could break on, and a plain string lets non-IANA values through the producer's replay. The experiment shows the pattern rejects a number, an offset, a bare city, an abbreviation and an empty string, and that both demo zones resolve in Intl to their own names. A built-in account in UTC or another slash-less zone would have argued for a looser pattern.

question: Q-011: an optional timeZone under additive-only leaves a consumer nothing to fall back on, and ADR-002 lets the web app use no other zone; what does profile-api@v2 promise about timeZone being present?

options.label: optional in the schema, a guarantee that every 200 profile carries it
options.consequence: The schema keeps timeZone optional, so the pre-touch fixtures still validate (the additive-only condition). options.consequence: Keeps the contract's text, at the cost of an encoding layer in every read and write for two characters no form can type.

options.label: leave it to the database
options.consequence: U+0000 becomes a 5xx (SQLSTATE 22021); an unpaired surrogate comes back as U+FFFD, so G8's exactly-as-sent fails silently.

question: How does the database make exactly one of simultaneous overlapping bookings win, with every loser answered 409 naming an overlapping booking and never a 5xx (booking-api@v1 G4 to G6; Q-051, Q-053)?

options.label: one transaction per booking under a per-room advisory lock: lock, read the earliest overlap, insert; cancel takes the same lock; the exclusion constraint stays as the invariant (D7)
options.consequence: Bookings of one room serialize; the conflict is read directly, so no SQLSTATE needs mapping in the normal path; the constraint still refuses any row that slips past, and a 23P01 or 40P01 is answered by the re-read.

options.label: the exclusion constraint alone: insert, on 23P01 or 40P01 re-read the earliest overlap, insert again when none is left
options.consequence: One statement and the schema as the only guard; under contention PostgreSQL may break deadlocks between the inserters one second at a time, and a loser can re-read before the winner commits.

options.label: SERIALIZABLE transactions that read and insert, retried on 40001
options.consequence: No lock to name, but retries under 20-way contention are unbounded by design and the overlap still needs the constraint to hold at any moment.

chosen: one transaction per booking under a per-room advisory lock: lock, read the earliest overlap, insert; cancel takes the same lock; the exclusion constraint stays as the invariant (D7)
why: Three runs of the experiment on PostgreSQL 17.11 with 20 simultaneous attempts: the lock settled 90 rounds with exactly one 201 and nineteen 409s naming it, the slowest round 71 ms, no deadlock. The constraint alone gave 40P01 to 76 of 570 and 38 of 190 losers in two runs, up to 19 s a round, and none in a third; with re-read and retry (the approach Q-053 sketched) the third run left 18 attempts unbooked after ten retries, one round took 215 s, and 219 deadlocks were detected. PRD v2 Success scripts 20 simultaneous attempts, so the lock's deterministic path leads; serializing one room's bookings costs nothing at two offices' volume. The cancel side takes the lock so a named conflict cannot vanish between the read and the answer (G6).

question: Q-058, Q-063: D1 notices expiry only when GET /api/me answers 401 on load, and cites profile-api@v1. booking-api@v1 G16 answers 401 UNAUTHORIZED at every endpoint, so a list, a Cancel or a Book can be the first request to meet an expired token (PRD v2 AC-2.3). How is D1 revisited?

options.label: any request carrying the token that answers 401 ends the session; D1 amended in place with a dated marker
options.consequence: GET /api/me on load and every booking-api@v1 call (Home's list and Cancel, Rooms' list and Book) clear the session and show Login with the AC-2.3 message; still no timer. D1 cites profile-api@v2 G7 and booking-api@v1 G16 instead of profile-api@v1, and keeps a marker naming what it said before.

options.label: keep D1 as written; a booking call's 401 shows an inline message
options.consequence: The user stays on a screen whose every action fails, with a message that does not match AC-2.3's, until the next reload.

options.label: a new decision superseding D1, D1 left as it was
options.consequence: The decisions list would hold a stale rule beside its replacement, and every phase context that cites D1 would carry the old one.

chosen: any request carrying the token that answers 401 ends the session; D1 amended in place with a dated marker
why: AC-2.3 asks that an expired session sends the user to Login with its message, wherever it is noticed; booking-api@v1 G16 and profile-api@v2 G7 make the 401 the same body and indistinguishable from an unknown token, so one handling fits all. The file's own convention amends decisions in place with a dated marker (D3, D5). profile-api@v1 stays stable, but D1's sentence is about the v2 endpoint the node now uses (Q-058). An ADR or contract that let the web app tell expiry from an unknown token would have changed the message per case.

question: Q-063, DEC-012: D4 says 'No router (RFC §6): the screen is a function of the session value'. With three screens, how does the app move between them, which screen shows after sign-in and on reload, and does Rooms keep a URL?

options.label: no router and no URL: the signed-in screen is held in memory; sign-in and reload show Home
options.consequence: The flow's signed-in state gains which screen shows, Home or Rooms; Book a room and Rooms' Home button switch it; only the session is stored (D2), so a reload on Rooms shows Home, and Rooms opens on today each time it shows. RFC-001 §6's choice holds with three screens; no package is added.

options.label: a hash per screen (#/rooms) read on load
options.consequence: A reload keeps the user on Rooms and the back button works, but the app gains URL parsing and a second source of truth beside the session, which RFC-001 §6 ruled out ('There are no URLs per screen').

options.label: a router package
options.consequence: Deep links and history for free, but a dependency and a structure RFC-001 §6 set aside, for one extra screen nothing links into.

chosen: no router and no URL: the signed-in screen is held in memory; sign-in and reload show Home
why: RFC-001 §6 (normative) made the app a function of state with no URLs per screen; PRD v2 Screens draws Home with Book a room and Rooms with a Home button and nothing that links into Rooms from outside. A reload showing Home costs one click, and PRD v2 AC-2.2 asks only that a reload keeps the user signed in. The RFC's two-screen premise is flagged upstream by the intake record (DEC-013). A PRD criterion to share or bookmark a Rooms date would have made the hash lead.

question: Q-061: the fixture stub matches String(input) against request.path, but the rooms fixtures' paths carry unencoded colons while URLSearchParams writes %3A. Does the client send the instants unencoded, or does the stub compare decoded URLs?

options.label: the client writes the instants unencoded; the stub keeps its exact match
options.consequence: The query is built as /api/rooms?from={from}&to={to} from toISOString() strings, whose characters are all legal in a query; the recorded call equals the fixture's path, so a test proves the exact request. booking-api@v1 accepts both forms.

options.label: the client uses URLSearchParams; the stub decodes both sides before comparing
options.consequence: The client uses the platform encoder, but the stub then accepts requests the fixtures do not name byte for byte, and every recorded path differs from its fixture's.

chosen: the client writes the instants unencoded; the stub keeps its exact match
why: The values are instants the client produced itself with toISOString() (digits, '-', ':', '.', 'T', 'Z'), so encoding adds nothing; booking-api@v1's GET /api/rooms section says the producer decodes either form. Keeping the stub exact keeps every web test a proof of the exact request the fixture names. A query value that could hold user text would have made the encoder lead.
evidence: booking-api@v1 Validation (consumers match on method and path)

question: Home lists my bookings that have not ended (booking-api@v1 G14), which includes one in progress that can no longer be cancelled (AC-6.2). Is Cancel shown on every listed booking, or hidden by the browser's clock once a booking has started?

options.label: Cancel on every listed booking; the backend's answer decides
options.consequence: A Cancel on a started booking gets 422 BOOKING_STARTED and the message 'That booking has already started, so it cannot be cancelled.', then the list is fetched again. The browser's clock decides nothing on Home.

options.label: hide Cancel when the browser's clock reads the start or later
options.consequence: No button that always fails, but the browser's clock then decides what the user may do, which ADR-002 Decision 5 does not list (it names only the Rooms screen's opening date and leaving past times out of the form), and a drifting laptop clock hides or shows the button wrongly near a start.

chosen: Cancel on every listed booking; the backend's answer decides
why: ADR-002 Decision 5 and booking-api@v1 G7 say the backend's clock decides and the browser's clock decides nothing, and the ADR names the only two uses it allows. The cost is one refused Cancel per in-progress booking, which the message explains. An ADR-002 sentence allowing the browser's clock to hide Cancel on a started booking would have flipped this.

question: PRD v2 fixes only AC-5.3's overlap message among the booking answers. What does the web app show for each other booking-api@v1 answer, given G18 (branch on error.code, never show error.message)?

options.label: one message per code in the web's own copy table, worded like the contract's messages where they read well
options.consequence: BOOKING_STARTED on Book 'That time has already started.', BOOKING_TOO_LONG 'A booking can last at most 8 hours.', BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD 'A booking can start at most 365 days ahead.', VALIDATION_FAILED on Book 'That booking is not valid. Check the times and the title.', a 201 'Booked.'; on Cancel, BOOKING_STARTED 'That booking has already started, so it cannot be cancelled.', BOOKING_NOT_FOUND 'That booking was already cancelled.', BOOKING_NOT_YOURS 'You can cancel only your own bookings.'; an empty list '(no bookings)'; 401 is D1 and anything unexpected D3's network message. The strings live in messages.ts, keyed by the client's reasons, so a backend wording change moves nothing.

options.label: show error.message as received
options.consequence: No copy to maintain, but G18 forbids it, the backend's wording becomes UI copy, and AC-5.3's sentence could not be written that way at all.

options.label: one generic failure message for every refusal
options.consequence: Least copy, but the user cannot tell a time that has started from a booking that is too long, and PRD v2's Goal (a free room in under a minute) suffers.

chosen: one message per code in the web's own copy table, worded like the contract's messages where they read well
why: D3 already set 'one message per failure' for sign-in; this extends it to the booking answers. booking-api@v1 G18 requires branching on the code; the contract's messages are plain and correct, so reusing their wording costs nothing and keeps the screens and the API consistent, while the web owns the strings. '(no bookings)' is PRD v2 Screens' own copy. Product copy for these cases in the PRD would have replaced the table.
evidence: PRD v2 AC-5.3, AC-6.2, AC-6.3, Screens

question: Q-061: the booking form may offer end times up to start + 8 hours and dates up to 365 days ahead, but the backend's answer decides; ADR-002 Decision 4 gives the form the picked date's quarter-hour instants and Decision 5 lets the browser's clock leave past times out. Which start and end times, and which dates, does the form offer?

options.label: starts after the browser's clock; ends up to start + 8 hours or the next date's start; any date
options.consequence: Starts: the picked date's quarter-hour instants later than the browser's clock. Ends: the quarter-hour instants after the start, up to whichever comes first, start + 8 hours of elapsed time (G9) or the start of the next date (labelled 'Fri 6 Nov 00:00'). The date input is not capped: a date past 365 days gets BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD from the backend, and past dates still show their bookings. A date with no start left says 'No times left on this date.'

options.label: every quarter-hour instant of the date for both, with no clock and no length filter
options.consequence: Simplest, but most of today's offers are refused as started, and ends past 8 hours are refused as too long.

options.label: also cap the date input at today + 365 days
options.consequence: Fewer refusals, but the Rooms list then cannot show far dates either, and the web would restate the backend's limit in a second place.

chosen: starts after the browser's clock; ends up to start + 8 hours or the next date's start; any date
why: ADR-002 Decision 4 confines the form to the picked date's instants and Decision 5 allows leaving past times out; offering only ends within G9 avoids a refusal the form can foresee without deciding anything (the backend still answers). The date input stays free because the same date drives the read-only rooms list (AC-4.2) and the backend decides how far ahead (G10). The experiment shows every 201 POST fixture's start and end are among the offers with the browser clock at the fixture's clock; book-started's start is not, so its test sets an earlier clock, as ADR-002 Consequences describe. A PRD rule allowing bookings across midnight would have extended the ends past the next date's start.

question: booking-api@v1's fixtures hold no my-bookings list containing a booking that a cancel fixture cancels (cancel-my-booking cancels ayu's ...031, which no list fixture names; my-bookings-budi lists ...011, ...013, ...015, ...016). question: Tier choice: the time functions (simple-login.web.6) are pure, which the skill's default puts at spot-check, but they carry AC-4.4 and every display rule of ADR-002 Decision 7. Which review tier?

question: Q-063, Isolation strategy: every web test runs with TZ set to a zone that is neither account's nor UTC (ADR-002 Consequences). Where is it set, and how is it proven?

options.label: TZ=Asia/Kolkata in the web's test and gate scripts, with a guard test
options.consequence: 'gate' becomes 'tsc --noEmit && TZ=Asia/Kolkata vitest run && vite build' and 'test' 'TZ=Asia/Kolkata vitest run'; a test fails unless the ambient zone resolves to Asia/Calcutta or Asia/Kolkata, so a run that loses the variable fails instead of passing on a laptop set to Jakarta or London. The root's npm test calls the web gate unchanged.

The guard test makes the setting checked rather than assumed, whichever way Vitest is started. Asia/Kolkata is ADR-002's own example. question: ADR-002 Decision 7: 'A time whose date, in the zone it is shown in, is not the date its line is about carries its own date.' On Rooms, the room's local times sit in the line of the picked date, so a London booking from 16:30 to 17:30 on 4 November shown to a Jakarta user on 5 November reads '(Wed 4 Nov 16:30 to Wed 4 Nov 17:30 in London)'. Is the rule applied literally, or does an end carry its date only when it differs from its start's?

options.consequence: Matches the ADR's sentence and its example ('23:00 to Fri 6 Nov 02:00'); the integration node, which reads the ADR and not this plan, asserts the same strings. Some room-local lines repeat a date.

options.label: an end carries its date only when it differs from its start's
options.consequence: Shorter lines ('(Wed 4 Nov 16:30 to 17:30 in London)'), but a reading the ADR does not state, which the integration node's browser tests could assert differently.

chosen: literally: each time against the line's date (the picked date on Rooms and in the overlap message, the start's date on Home)
why: The ADR states one rule per time and DEC-032 put it in the ADR so the integration node asserts the same strings; a web-only refinement would split the two. The experiment gives the exact strings for the three rooms fixtures, including the repeated date on Kew's Handover line. An ADR-002 amendment shortening the room-local form would change it; it is flagged in the report for the owner.

question: How many phases does the PRD v2 append to simple-login.integration take, and how is the work split between them?

options.label: three: rig and service tests, Home, Rooms
options.consequence: simple-login.integration.3 builds the PostgreSQL rig, the booking-api@v1 replay and the API-level Success tests (~340 lines, 7 tasks); .4 adds the time helpers and the Home tests (AC-2.1, AC-2.5, US-6, ~250 lines); .5 the Rooms tests with London's clock-change days (US-4, US-5, AC-4.4, ~300 lines). Each fits one sitting; .4 and .5 differ in tier, so no merge candidate.

options.label: two: rig, then every browser test
options.consequence: The browser phase would be ~550 lines and 10 or more tasks, over one review sitting.

options.label: four: clock-change days on their own
options.consequence: Rooms (~200 lines) and clock-change days (~120 lines) would share tier and contracts with no third phase depending on one alone, and merged fit one sitting: a merge candidate pair under the sizing floor with no named reason to keep it split.

chosen: three: rig and service tests, Home, Rooms
why: Interfaces-first puts the shared rig first: the database of its own, the service started through its documented command, the API helpers, then the tests that use them. The browser work splits by screen because Home's tests make their bookings through booking-api@v1 and need no Rooms screen, while the Rooms tests need the time helpers .4 writes. Sizes are estimates from the shipped e2e files (414 lines today) and the strings the tests must compute.

question: Bookings now persist across runs of the suite (Q-073): how does a test run get a database, or slots, that no earlier run or developer has touched?

options.label: a database of its own per run
options.consequence: Playwright's global setup runs `npm --prefix backend run db:up`, then drops and re-creates `meeting_rooms_e2e` on the backend's Compose service through the `pg` package (a root devDependency) and starts the service with DATABASE_URL naming it. Every run starts empty and `meeting_rooms` keeps the developer's bookings. It assumes the service creates its tables in an empty database at start, which no contract states: a request entry asks.

options.label: the default database, free slots found through booking-api@v1
options.consequence: No new dependency and no assumption, but the tests write into the developer's `meeting_rooms`, a developer's booking can take a slot a test computed, and no test can assert '(no bookings)' or an exact Rooms day.

options.label: a database per test file
options.consequence: Stronger isolation, but the worker-scoped service would restart for every file, and the rig would manage several databases for no criterion that needs it.

chosen: a database of its own per run
why: The conventions' Local database section already gives the backend's tests databases of their own on that service and keeps them off `meeting_rooms`; the integration's tests do the same. Creating and dropping a database is a server operation that touches none of the backend's tables, so the schema stays the backend's (Q-073 rules out writing its tables). The `meeting_rooms` user can create databases (the backend's tests do; booking-store-postgres measured 36 ms a database). Inside a run, each test books on dates and rooms no other test uses. The gap is whether `npm --prefix backend start` creates its tables in an empty database: recorded as a request on booking-api@v1, with contingent phases none, because either answer keeps the phase set (a separate schema command would be run by the same global setup). A backend answer that the schema exists only through Compose's first-start scripts would have made the default database with free slots the better choice.

question: How does the browser suite's backend fixture start and restart the real service once it runs on PostgreSQL?

options.label: npm --prefix backend start, in its own process group
options.consequence: The rig depends only on the command the conventions document (needs the database up, reads DATABASE_URL, PORT pinned to 3000); a restart stops the whole group, as scripts/dev.mjs already does, and waits for port 3000 to close.

options.label: keep spawning backend/src/server.ts
options.consequence: One process to stop, as shipped, but the rig names a file inside backend/, which this node does not own and whose start-up may change with PostgreSQL.

chosen: npm --prefix backend start, in its own process group
why: simple-login.integration does not own any code under backend/ (node header), and the conventions' Local database section names `npm --prefix backend start` as the service's start command. scripts/dev.mjs shows the process-group stop works for npm-started children on this laptop. Evidence that the backend's start script adds work a test must not pay for on every restart would have kept the direct spawn.

question: Where do the root scripts start PostgreSQL for `npm run dev`, `npm test` and `npm run e2e`?

options.label: chained in package.json, and again in the e2e global setup
options.consequence: `dev` becomes `npm --prefix backend run db:up && node scripts/dev.mjs`; `test` runs `db:up` before the dev runner's test and the browser suite; the global setup runs it too, so `npm run e2e` works alone. scripts/dev.mjs and its tested process handling stay as shipped. No root db:down: the README names `npm --prefix backend run db:down`.

options.label: inside scripts/dev.mjs
options.consequence: One place for `dev`, but it changes the tested runner, its tests then need Docker for the failure case too, and `test` and `e2e` still need their own call.

chosen: chained in package.json, and again in the e2e global setup
why: Q-074 and the conventions say every node starts the database through `npm --prefix backend run db:up`, which picks `docker compose` or `docker-compose` and returns once healthy; on this laptop only docker-compose 5.6.1 exists, so no root script calls Docker itself. db:up is idempotent, so calling it twice in `npm test` costs a health check.

question: Which booking-api@v1 fixtures does the proxy replay extend to, against the real service on the real clock?

options.label: the 15 decided before any clock or stored-booking rule
options.consequence: Eight 400s, four 401s (my-bookings-expired-token through the shipped restart), cancel-unknown, cancel-malformed-id and book-too-long: 24 exact replays with the shipped nine. book-too-long holds because BOOKING_TOO_LONG is order 3 of POST, before the clock's orders 4 and 5.

options.label: the 14 Q-069 named
options.consequence: Leaves out book-too-long, a fixture the running service answers as written under every clock and state.

options.label: all 35 through a seeded database
options.consequence: Not possible: the service runs on the real clock and the fixtures fix theirs; seeding fixed ids would write the backend's tables.

chosen: the 15 decided before any clock or stored-booking rule
why: A reference model of the contract's check orders answered each fixture's request under 7 clocks from 2026-11-01 to 2028-11-01 and two stored states (none; 78,912 random-id bookings in every room): exactly 15 answer as written in every condition. Q-069's count of 14 missed book-too-long. The rule, not only the list, goes into the phase so a later fixture is classified the same way.

question: How do the PRD v2 Success tests run: 20 simultaneous attempts give one booking, and a restart keeps every booking?

options.label: API tests at the service's address, five rounds
options.consequence: Node's fetch sends 20 requests at once to http://127.0.0.1:3000 (10 with ayu's token, 10 with budi's), five rounds, the fifth with 20 different ranges that all share one quarter hour; each round gives one 201 and nineteen 409 BOOKING_CONFLICT whose conflict is the winner, and GET /api/rooms then lists one booking. The restart test books for both accounts, restarts the service, sees the old tokens answer 401, signs in again and finds every booking with its id.

options.label: one round through the dev proxy
options.consequence: Matches the PRD's wording literally, but the Vite proxy's connection handling sits between the attempts and the service, and one round proves less about a race than five.

chosen: API tests at the service's address, five rounds
why: The Success criterion is about the service and its database (booking-api@v1 G5, G6, G17); the dev proxy adds nothing to it, and the browser's view of AC-5.4 gets its own two-browser test in .5. The backend's experiment settled 20 attempts in under 100 ms, so five rounds cost under a second. A sign that the owner wants the proxy path under load would have moved the attempts behind it.

question: Which scripted test covers the criteria that turn on the backend's clock (PRD v2 AC-5.5, AC-6.2's started case, AC-6.1's booking in progress) and the one no screen reaches (AC-6.3), when the service runs on the real clock?

options.label: service tests now, the backend's replay for a started booking
options.consequence: AC-5.5: an API test books the current quarter hour (422 BOOKING_STARTED), and a browser test holds only the browser's clock five minutes before that quarter hour so the form offers it. AC-6.2's started case and AC-6.1's in-progress booking: the backend's replay of cancel-started and my-bookings-budi under its injected clock, on its real PostgreSQL, which the root `npm test` runs. AC-6.3: an API test (403 BOOKING_NOT_YOURS). No test waits for a start.

options.label: a test that waits for a booking to start
options.consequence: Proves AC-6.2's started case end to end, at up to 15 minutes of waiting on every run.

options.label: an opt-in slow script for the waiting test
options.consequence: End to end on demand, but a criterion outside `npm test` is easy to stop running.

chosen: service tests now, the backend's replay for a started booking
why: ADR-002 Decision 5 makes the backend's injected clock decide, and booking-api@v1 Validation leaves the clock-bound fixtures to the producer's replay; that replay is a scripted test against the real routes and a real PostgreSQL, run by the root `npm test`, so PRD v2 Success's 'every acceptance criterion passes in a scripted test' holds. Booking a time that has started needs no waiting at all, so AC-5.5 is end to end. The browser-clock technique was checked in the installed Chrome. Home never lists another user's booking, so AC-6.3 is reachable only through the API. An owner who reads Success as 'end to end in the browser' would want the opt-in waiting script.

question: PRD 1's 'Home within 3 seconds of Sign in' is gone from PRD v2 Success, but the shipped e2e/login.spec.ts still asserts it as AC-1.1 (Q-072): keep the assertion as a regression check, or drop it?

options.label: drop the timing assertion
options.consequence: The AC-1.1 test asserts AC-1.1 only (the right password reaches Home); the suite holds no assertion PRD v2 does not ask for, and a wall-clock limit leaves a browser suite that now also starts PostgreSQL.

options.label: keep it, renamed as a regression check
options.consequence: Catches a pathological slow-down of sign-in at no cost today, but keeps a timing assertion no requirement backs, and its failures would be read as a PRD failure.

chosen: drop the timing assertion
why: PRD v2 Success names three criteria and none is a time to Home; its Goal's 'under a minute' is a person's time to find and book a room, which no script measures. The test name claims the 3 seconds is part of AC-1.1, which it never was. A PRD v2 performance target, or a history of this check catching a regression, would have kept it.

question: Which London clock-change days do the AC-4.4 browser tests use, and what do they book on them, when the service runs on the real clock and booking-api@v1 accepts starts at most 365 days ahead?

options.label: both next days, booked when within 365 days
options.consequence: The tests take the next last Sunday of March and of October strictly after today's date in London; on each they check the form and book Thames (00:30 to 02:30 on the March day, 01:30 BST to 01:30 GMT on the October day) when that start is within 365 days of the real clock. The nearer day always is (at most 217.02 days); the farther one is not for about six days in some years, and then the test checks that day's form and Rooms lines only and records an annotation.

options.label: only the next change day
options.consequence: Always bookable, but one run proves either the 23-hour or the 25-hour day, never both, for half a year at a time.

options.label: fixed dates
options.consequence: Pass, and then cannot be booked: 2026-10-25 has already gone (ADR-002 Consequences).

chosen: both next days, booked when within 365 days
why: AC-4.4 names both change days, and they fail differently (a skipped hour, a repeated hour). Scanning every hour from 2026-11-01 to 2032 found the nearer day's booking at most 217.02 days ahead, and the farther one beyond 365 days only in two spans of about six days (March 2029, October 2031); from 2026-11-01 both are bookable (147 and 364 days). Viewing a date needs no limit, since GET /api/rooms caps no range.

question: How do the browser tests know the exact strings to expect, when their dates follow the real clock?

options.label: a helper of the suite's own, Intl with an explicit zone
options.consequence: e2e/time.ts computes day ranges, quarter hours, the next change days and ADR-002 Decision 7's strings from Intl with the zone as an argument; its own tests pin ADR-002's examples and the 2027 change days. Two independent readings of ADR-002 must agree.

options.label: import the web app's time functions
options.consequence: No second implementation, but the suite then tests web/src against itself and couples to code this node does not own.

options.label: literal strings only
options.consequence: Impossible for dates that move with the clock, and wrong across London's offset change during the year.

chosen: a helper of the suite's own, Intl with an explicit zone
why: The node does not own code under web/, and a test that imports the formatter it checks proves nothing about it. web-time-display showed Intl alone reproduces every rule and PRD v2's example strings; the helper's tests pin the same strings. Where the web's mechanism is its own choice (whether Book is disabled for an empty title, say), the tests assert the PRD outcome through booking-api@v1 (no booking made) rather than the mechanism.

question: In which time zone do the browser, the test runner and the service they start run, and how is it set?

options.label: Asia/Kolkata, set in playwright.config.ts
options.consequence: The config sets `process.env.TZ = "Asia/Kolkata"` before anything reads the clock, so the runner, its workers and the service they start inherit it whichever way Playwright is started, and `use.timezoneId: "Asia/Kolkata"` sets the browser's. A time computed in the ambient zone is off by 1:30 or 5:30 from both accounts' and fails.

options.label: Asia/Kolkata, set in the npm script
options.consequence: `TZ=Asia/Kolkata playwright test` covers `npm run e2e` only; `npx playwright test` would run in the laptop's zone.

options.label: another zone
options.consequence: Any zone that is neither account's nor UTC works; a different one from the web node's tests buys nothing.

chosen: Asia/Kolkata, set in playwright.config.ts
why: ADR-002 Consequences names Asia/Kolkata (+05:30) for every node's tests and the browser's zone for the browser tests; the node's Isolation strategy says the same. integration-browser-clock confirmed timezoneId gives the page Asia/Calcutta (an alias), offset -330, in the installed Chrome. The service inheriting TZ also shows it never uses its process's zone (ADR-002 Decision 3).

question: request `booking-api@v1`: when `npm --prefix backend start` runs with `DATABASE_URL` naming an empty database on simple-login.backend's Compose service, does the service create its tables and the four pre-loaded rooms there before it listens, as it must for `meeting_rooms` on a fresh clone?
